utterances.text: About three years ago, two or three years ago. It's probably more like three years ago that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abdurahmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Defence is ready for the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, before you proceed, I'd just like to give you some guidance that's not especially for cross-examining, but you raised a question on whether the Prosecution could be more precise as far as the time frame was concerned earlier. It may be of some guidance for you that whenever a question might create confusion as far as the time is concerned, so we're talking about confrontation lines during periods that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. could create confusion, it could make the answers also ambiguous. Since the witness was testifying about a single incident, the question when this incident actually happened, it's not necessary to put that question in the beginning of the questioning on the incident to the witness. If you would have had reasons to believe that there might have been two similar incidents, then, of course, your objection would be totally justified. But since that was at least not the basis for your objection, that's the reason why I allowed the Prosecution to continue the questioning. So if we are talking about time frames, it's always done when there's a risk for confusion and ambiguous answers. Please proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will be paying attention, and I believe that we will understand why I had made this remark earlier. And I will demonstrate it, I hope, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon. Thank you for coming. Thank you for the clarity of your answers that you have given and that you will hopefully give me when I ask the questions now. During which period were you in the army? Could you specify that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Until Dayton was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I understand the end, but when did you start?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was mobilised in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for this answer. As far as I can remember, that was in November 1995 that Dayton was signed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: When it was signed and -- when it was signed, then we were released from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You do not remember, sir, when you were released from the army, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. When Dayton was signed, we were then released.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. But could I then assume that you were in the army throughout the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you didn't tell us, I believe, whether you were wearing a uniform in the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, I was not wearing a uniform. I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That was not my question, sir. I'm going to rephrase it. I'm going to ask you it again. Have you understood it, or have you not understood the question?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: You can ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question was the following: Did you have a uniform at the beginning of the war? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not have a uniform for two years or longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. So I can conclude that the army did not issue you with a uniform during the first two or three years of the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not that it did not issue it; it's just we didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That's what I was saying. The soldiers did not wear uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, would one be able to tell you apart from others if you were not wearing a uniform, tell you apart as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis. I'm sorry. I was just looking at my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's okay, Mr. President. I would object to this question. It calls for speculation on behalf of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just... [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just rereading on my screen the answer. The objection is denied. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was shooting at the civilians. We were not wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, that was not my question. I did not ask you whether civilians were targeted. My question, I believe, was very clear. What was -- was it possible to -- visually, to tell apart a civilian from a soldier, a civilian who is not dressed as a soldier from a soldier who is dressed as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Abdurahmanovic, perhaps I could help you. You told the Court that for a rather long period of time, although being in the military, you did not wear a uniform. The question was how someone could see, since you were not wearing a uniform, whether you were civilian or military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we were on duty, I had clothes that I was going to the line in. This was a civilian jacket, and I had insignia on it, the insignia of the BH army on it. When I got off duty, then I would change my clothes. I would leave my jacket and my old jeans, and I would put new clothes on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us what was the size of the insignia that you just told us about?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: About that size, it's -- it was a coat of arms. We would wear it either on our shoulders or on the chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you said you could not remember the date of the incident, but that you were certain that there was no exchange of fire on that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you read English?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. President, we will need the help of the interpreters once again. I'm going to submit a number of documents to the witness that are also -- that originate also from the UNPROFOR, and we know that these documents cannot have their source contested. They are of the same kind of documents as those that we looked at last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have copies for the translators?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are enough copies to go around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would have the same objection that we had when this procedure was used last week. It's our view that a foundation needs to be laid and we need to ascertain whether or not this witness is familiar with UNPROFOR SIT reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what questions will be about these documents. So I would say we first proceed until we come at a point where you think that the question suggested a type of knowledge which cannot be expected from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, I will ask you questions that are not directly related to these documents, just to gain time. May I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if we bear in mind the relatively small size of Sarajevo, when shots were fired from a relative distance, were you able to hear them?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: We could hear artillery, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You mean artillery -- that means mortar, I believe?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, I believe that you will have before you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the witness has -- is able to see this document. If that is not the case, I will -- I will ask if the interpreters can help with this, and I'm sure that it will go very well. Thank you very much in advance. For the transcript, this is a document which is reference number ERN 91977, for the -- for page number 2 that we will have a look at, and then of course, 76, ending -- ERN number ending with 76 for the page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I will now quote you a sentence that will be translated to you and then I will ask a question. This is what the military observers are saying. For the interpreters, I'm quoting page 2, item 2, 1, [In English] "The town reported people on the [microphone not activated] side at 100315 hours," I think, "three mortar rounds fell close to the PTT building. No damage reported. Situation on Igman is relatively stable." [Interpretation] Could we perhaps have this translated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the interpreter [microphone not activated] -- You want to start at the "The town reported"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this was interpreted at the same time. I'm not sure whether that was the case. This is my question. Was this done?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear this? I believe I am being told that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not clear from the question what the time frame is that my learned colleague is referring to or the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the only thing until now what he did is to read a part of a document, as far as I understand, and -- if he, for example, check on whether the witness has written it himself but the date is not yet in play, I would say, so therefore please continue with the -- but the first thing I would like to know is when Mr. Piletta-Zanin read the English text of page 2, was it immediately translated, and could you follow it in your language, Mr. Abdurahmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So I have just read to you a text from which number of things can be seen, that there was a -- there was a number of mortar shells fired on the city of Sarajevo, that is on the PTT building. Sir, are you still certain that on the day of the attack, there were no -- there was no artillery fire, mortar fire? And in order to be absolutely precise, we are talking about the 10th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no shooting in Cengic Vila, that's what I said. And if there was any other shooting or fire, but, for instance, if it was downtown, I couldn't have heard it because this is maybe seven, eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, what is the distance between the PTT building and the neighbourhood of Cengic Vila?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Which PTT building? Do you mean the main post office building in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly 5 or 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will tender, if we are allowed, this document which refers to another question that I'm going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: At least 120 shells that were fired on that day, and mortars. And, Witness, you are telling me that you did not hear anything?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: We did not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, are we talking of January or the summer of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This should be the 10th of January, 1994, but we will check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Check. I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The dates that we have coming from the Prosecution are the 10th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: On page 83, line 16 or so, I think that the witness spoke about summertime. Let me check.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, do check because that's the reason why I was asking about the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I don't know which is the date. The witness said summertime. You are talking about January. That's wintertime. So I am a little bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that the Defence is aware of the fact there are a number of different seasons, and we will have a check. But I believe that the incident we are talking about is dated the 10th of January, 1994, in the documents that are coming from the Registry itself, because I have here a Registry number. So if we are talking about the incident number 19, but it is true that the numbering of the incidents having changed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was not aware of the date of January for this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you for drawing our attention to it. Mr. President, I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you were in service in the army, did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did. When I would go to the position, to the line, I would then be given a rifle -- I would then be given a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you left your weapon in the trenches or on the line, was this weapon used by others?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would be taken over by others. The next shift would take it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am coming back to the question of the trenches. You said you knew the front lines very well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know where the front lines were, where the lines were. I knew who held what.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, were these front lines also present by the fact that there were trenches there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, we knew that Hrasno Brdo was held by them. The actual height of the hill and the houses around, that meant they held it. And we were just below.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But were there trenches there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: That depends where and how. There were sometimes trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: As far as you know, and to your recollection, do you know where these trenches were?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were trenches in Nedzarici, for instance. And then on the Zuc hill, there were trenches. On the Stup hill out of Sarajevo. Then there were towards Trebevic, Mount Trebevic. That's where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is that all? Were there other locations where there were trenches?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: All around Sarajevo. Yes, somewhere there would be a trench and somewhere there wouldn't be a trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say "all around Sarajevo," Witness, do you mean that this was practically all around the city itself?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Could you tell us to which brigade you belonged throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: To the 102nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What you mean, that was the 102nd motorised brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I see you are perfectly informed. Thank you. And where was the headquarters or where was the general staff of the 102 motorised brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: In Zica. It's a company at Alipasino.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us where in Alipasino? Would you be able to show us on the map where the headquarters of the 102nd motorised was?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to ask the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. usher to find a neutral map, if we still have copies which are unmarked of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it's up to you to tender whatever neutral map. It's not a matter of inviting the Registry. But let's try to see how we can solve your problem, but we can't rely upon maps that have already been admitted into evidence because we can't change them any more. But perhaps there would be one way or another to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you in advance. The number of the map is 3644. And it should be a virgin map, a map without any markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you refer to the big black and white map? Yes, but of course we have no -- we could show it to the witness. But if you have no other copies, it could not then be marked. So what is your intention?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to confer with my colleague, please, five seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that all that we can do is to do it this way: We shall put this map on the ELMO, on the monitor. We shall ask the witness to point at the location of the headquarters, and we shall then orally describe -- describe orally for the transcript the location which he has pointed at. We do have a map, but it is already marked. But what is important for us is not the exhibit itself; it's just the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you then use this black and white big map or, if you're not going to tender it into evidence, perhaps you could use, because it's more clear, if the location you're looking for is on this map, perhaps the map that has been admitted into evidence, P3100.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Very good. Yes, that will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Relatively much detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, to your right, you can see a map which I hope is useful. Will you please have a look at it, and with the pointer which you should also have somewhere at your disposal - that's it - will you please point -- perhaps we could blow up this image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a zoom, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is. Here it is. That's Zica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: For the transcript, we can say that the witness is pointing at an area which is to the right of a rectangle which is to the left on the map, so slightly to the right of it. And it is after also to the right from the words "Alipasin Most". So thank you, Witness. This is where the headquarters of the 102nd motorised brigade was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you now, in relation to this brigade -- no, no, no, I withdraw. How strong was the brigade, more or less?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, but roughly an order of magnitude, a few hundred, a few thousand?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: A few hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you now point, please, at the location of the barracks; that is, the places where soldiers could sleep. I mean members of your brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: But we didn't sleep in barracks. That is not where we slept. We slept either on the front line or at home. You spent four days on the front line, and then you have four days off and you're at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But you, personally. So at times you slept on the front line and at times you slept at home. Am I interpreting your words right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And what were the facilities at the front line allowing the soldiers to sleep?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Old houses, derelict houses. A house which is on the front line, that is where you sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do I understand you well, if I say that soldiers on the front line slept in private houses; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But you used the word old houses, "stari kuce." Do I take it to mean private houses, old private houses?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Old private houses. Nobody living in it so we go in and sleep there, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, we are talking about residential houses, about --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is houses which were inhabited previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm talking about houses in which people lived earlier.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, earlier. Those were residential houses, houses in which people lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, on the front line, to your knowledge, did your army also have any heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no, no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm not talking about tanks. I'm talking, generally speaking, about heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: We had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, are you telling me that your army did not have any heavy weapons in its possession? Is that how I should understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there would be a mortar here and there, an old one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, so we are now making some progress. Witness, did you also know, the rocket launchers, were they used in correlation with the private vehicles? That is, were they used with the assistance of Golfs, that is Volkswagen Golfs? That is, the launchers would be mounted on Golf cars so that they could be moved and fired? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not. No. I know we never had any rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My last question, Witness: Do you know if there were batteries which would be functioning on the side of your army or within the city?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My last question: Can you please try to remember when did the -- this incident that you told us about come to pass, that you talked to us -- told us about when you were examined by the Prosecution. Was it summer or was it wintertime?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was summertime because it was a very nice day. It was sunny. It was not cold. We were wearing T-shirts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do not have any further questions. But, of course, we shall be tendering the two pages which I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that. Mr. Mundis, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Abdurahmanovic, in response to a question from my learned colleague, you mentioned that you had insignias which you placed on your jacket. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you obtain these insignias? Where did you get them from?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: We were given them in our unit as the army was being formed. We were issued with them, so that we would have something that would show that we were the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if everyone in your unit was issued such an insignia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if such insignias were issued to other units of the ABiH, at least in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was an honour for us to wear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not there was a ceasefire in effect on the day that Edin was shot?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember. I do not know if there was any ceasefire, but I know it was calm, not a shot could be heard, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abdurahmanovic. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Judge Nieto-Navia will now question you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Could you please describe for us the insignia, the size and everything on the insignias?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was about that big, Bosnian coat of arms with lilies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: For the transcript, I'm sorry, we need the size. Could you say how many square centimetres or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about ten -- ten by six or seven centimetres, just with -- ten by six, ten by seven, roughly, and it said "BH Army," and there was the coat of arms with lilies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd nevertheless like to ask you two short questions. The first one has to do with what you said, namely, that you had met your friend during the war. Was he also a military man, a soldier? Was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was a child. He was 15 or 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But then if I understand you well, you said, "I met this friend, we struck friendship during the war."

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why, yes, because he lived near that shop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. And the car which came to take your friend away, do you remember what make was it -- it was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Golf, a Golf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was a Golf?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same make as the one that the Defence counsel had in mind when he asked you if those Golf cars were used to mount launchers on them? Would that be the same make?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he mentioned a Golf, but I don't know that Golf which carried the launchers. I never saw that. I mean, can't be a Golf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that car was near the place of the incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was my friend's, and it was parked right there in front of the shop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it was just one bullet that was fired or were there several?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ABDURAHMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one bullet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no more questions for you, Mr. Abdurahmanovic, I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague. It's quite a journey for you. This Court only can take decisions if this Court is well informed about what happened at the time of the charges. Answering the questions of the Prosecution and the Defence helps this Court to take the decisions which it will have to take. I thank you very much for coming to this strange environment for you, and I wish you a good journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you lead the witness out of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, we have, I think, some documents or at least objects to be admitted into evidence. First of all the video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video is P3280G.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I think we have the 360 degree electronic photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it "I" or was it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe it's "F," Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I did write down "F" as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe we have the document tendered by the -- by the Defence which is not prenumbered but it would then get number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D34. Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prosecution would object to the admission of this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for what reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On the grounds that, if I understand my learned colleague correctly, he's introducing this as a means of impeaching the witness with respect to whether or not he recalled hearing any shells being fired on the day in question. I would draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the operative paragraph that Mr. Piletta-Zanin read out. It's unclear from that in which direction the shells were fired, whether they were incoming or outgoing shells. It's a bit unclear as to the actual date that this document refers to, the operative sentence reading "at 10 0315 HRS," which could be the 10th of January at 0315 in the morning. And certainly the witness was not referring to that time period. Also, on the grounds again that the witness had never seen this document and there was, in our opinion, no proper foundation laid with respect to this document. Those would be our objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I thought that this was -- that the last time we agreed on this document, and this is precisely -- is exactly the same document. It covers the period that we are interested in, and that is the 10th of January, 1994. And this is the first minutes of that day up to 23 hours, again, until the very last minute of that one day. And that the same thing is -- and rather, just one mortar. Even if there was just one shot fired from a mortar, that would be enough to bring into question the testimony. And I do not think that UNPROFOR could be called anything but completely impartial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I suggest that we take this issue on the admission of the document tomorrow. Perhaps one question in order to -- as far as I can see it, because I do understand -- apart from the confusion about the date of the incident, as far as I see, the mortar rounds you quoted are situated at a time. As far as I understand it, it's 3.15 in the morning. If someone says they didn't hear anything in the day and just in the beginning of the night, I'm still -- I mean, if you're just concentrating on --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but let me remind you: If we are looking at tendering this page, it is that altogether there were 120 rounds, but it does not say that they all happened at 3.15. It covers the whole day, as we can see from the first page, and that is why we wish both pages to be annexed and tendered. Evidently, we had one incident with two shots at the PTT building -- no, excuse me, three, three mortar shots at 3.15 in the morning. As for the remaining 120 -- or rather, 117, I suppose they are spaced out over the whole day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I must admit to you that I'm a bit uncertain about what part exactly has been read to the witness, and that might be of major importance. I mean, if you read also the 120, but I'm not quite sure about that. Therefore, I have to find the exact place where you did read, if anyone could be of any assistance so that at least it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we should try to find it in the French transcript and see whether we can succeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't find the exact... Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps I can help, with your leave. In my English transcript - I'll try to be very precise - it is page 96, 96, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So page 96, line 6, and it begins, "At least 120 shells" -- this is a translation, but that is what I said, Mr. President. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. Let's just see quite precisely because we have to decide on the admissibility what exactly -- what you did read to the...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The passage that I read, Mr. President, was the passage right -- which is under 2A --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: It is page 94, line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I just found it. Let me just read it. And if you check in the French transcript, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it reads -- and I start at page 94, line 10: "Witness, I will now quote you a sentence that will be translated to you, and then I will ask a question. This is what military observers are saying. For the interpreters, I'm quoting page 2, item 2.1. And then [In English] [Previous translation continued]... Reported people on the side at 10 03.15 hours. I think three mortar rounds fell close to the" -- and then I think it's the PTT building. "No damage reported. Situation on Igman is relatively stable." So that's what you read to the witness. And it was later on, I think that's on page 96, that after the witness had responded to various questions on the issue you quoted, one of the last questions was "Which PTT building?" said the witness. "Do you mean the main post office in Sarajevo?" You said that's what you meant. The answer was then possibly 5 or 6 kilometres. And then Mr. Piletta-Zanin: "Mr. President, we will tender if we are allowed this document which refers to another question I'm going to ask you. At least 120 shells were fired that were on that day, and mortars. And, Witness, you are telling me that you did not hear anything." And he said he did not hear anything. So it's in the second part where you are not reading but referring to part of the statement. So I do understand that that's what you say is the relevance, that also the 120 shells which would not have been heard by the witness. And they are not in time located at 3.15 in the morning, but more in general during that day. Do I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As a matter of fact, this is a two-tiered question, and both have to do with this document. And I think it transpires rather clearly what the witness said. We asked the witness what he heard, and he said he did not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I told you, I think we'll have to decide. Three Judges will discuss, and we will give you the decision tomorrow. Is there any other observation to be made on this specific issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a final observation, Mr. President: I'll rely on what I mentioned earlier, but my learned colleague has said that the other 117 rounds could have come evenly spaced throughout the day. It's equally plausible that they all could have come in a five-minute period 0400 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we are more or less discussing the probative value of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, probative value and admission are two different issues, but we'll consider the matter and we'll decide tomorrow on the admission into evidence of this document. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one last comment: The Defence has never received any information concerning the manner in which the 360-degree computer image was produced, and we should like to know how reliable, how credible, and so on and so forth this image is. And I believe that some day or other, not now, but the Prosecutor should give us some more information as to that. Thank you very much in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would -- we'll consider that. I do understand that the first time, we had some explanation as far as the creation of both the video and the photos were concerned, if I am -- if my recollection is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your recollection is, indeed, correct, Mr. President. And the Prosecution is intending on calling the witness who actually produced both the video -- or did the editing on the videos and on the 360 photos for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. And of course, he will be able to answer the questions of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Mundis. We'll then adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
